2bigha API Integration Handbook: Every other operation in this handbook is called the exact same way: same URL, same { "query": "...",
"variables": {...} } body shape, same two auth headers on every call — only the text of query and the
contents of variables change. The “Input” and “Response” fields documented for every operation in the

Every operation in this handbook (aside from a small number of genuinely public/anonymous queries, called out
individually where they occur) requires an authenticated identity. The CRM integration authenticates with a
single Key/Secret pair, sent as two headers on every request — there is no login call, no session token, and no
2bigha issues the CRM a long-lived Key ID (a public identifier, safe to appear in logs) and a Secret Key (shown
once at creation time, treated like a password from then on), scoped to a dedicated “CRM Integration” service
account rather than to any individual human admin. The CRM sends both headers on every single request
instead of a session token — there is no login step, no session expiry, and nothing to refresh.
Note: We will provide you the Authentication document separately.

column2: Always check errors in the response body, not just data.
Most error objects carry a machine-readable extensions.code (e.g. UNAUTHENTICATED, FORBIDDEN,
BAD_USER_INPUT) in addition to a human-readable message — prefer branching on code where present.
Many response types in this API also carry their own application-level status envelope in addition to the
transport-level GraphQL response — most commonly a message: String and a STATUS_CODES field (typed
inconsistently across modules as either Int or String — this inconsistency is called out again in each
section’s Shared Types & Enums subsection). Treat STATUS_CODES as a secondary, business-level status
signal layered on top of (not a replacement for) the standard GraphQL errors array — check both.
Pagination is not fully uniform across the API: most list queries accept some combination of page, limit,
and/or offset, and return a totalCount alongside result. The exact accepted combination is
documented per-operation since it varies module to module.
Core CRM API — Leads, the Lead 360 view (properties/agent/lead/usage/status), Notes, Groups,
Property Management. This is the heart of the schema and almost certainly where CRM integration
work should start: it’s the single richest source of the “lead with property metadata and subscription
metadata” view the CRM needs to display.
Client & Agent Sync — the two operations that keep an identity in sync between the two systems:
creating the underlying client/customer record a lead needs (adminCreateUser) and creating/reading
agent accounts (createAdmin and friends) so 2bigha and the CRM agree on who the agents are.
Property API — creating and reading properties: the “create the property in 2bigha from the CRM” flow,
plus the read/search operations the CRM needs to display property data and keep it current.
Property Management (PM) Service API — the separate B2C paid property-management subscription
product; scoped here to what a CRM agent needs to look up a lead’s PM plan/visit/verification/ticket
status, with a short inventory of the many internal PM operations that fall outside the CRM’s integration
scope.

2bigha API Integration Handbook: Property Management (PM) Service — Subscription, Visit & Verification
This section covers the PROPERTY_MANAGEMENT GraphQL domain.
What PM is. Property Management (PM) is a large, separate B2C subscription product bolted onto the 2bigha
platform: a user pays up front for a plan, and in exchange 2bigha’s own operations staff — Regional Managers
(RM) and Field Agents, working under Super Admins — physically visit the property, verify legal documents,
produce inspection reports, and run a support-ticket desk for the life of the subscription. The commercial model
is prepaid and unbound-first: a pm_user_subscriptions row goes ACTIVE the moment Razorpay payment clears,
with no property attached yet (an “unbound” subscription/credit). Only when the user (or an admin) submits a
property via createManagedPropertyByUser / pmAdminCreateManagedPropertyOrder does the subscription bind to
that property, start its plan clock (startDate/endDate), and seed its visit quota (pm_visit_tracking). From there, a
long internal workflow runs: Super Admin assigns an RM → RM assigns a Field Agent (and, separately, a Legal
Manager) → visits get requested/scheduled/executed with GPS check-in/out → the agent submits a report →
the RM reviews it section-by-section → legal/pre-verification steps complete → the property is APPROVED.
Along the way the RM can upsell paid add-ons via a feasibility-check-then-quote flow, and either side can raise
